newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen higher at US noon, vaulting above 118.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen higher at US noon, vaulting above 118.

text.p: The dollar vaulted the key 118-yen level just after midday while it also shook off late morning selling pressure versus the mark in a session dominated by cross activity, traders said.

"This is quite normal at this time of day, and as soon as (European dealers) go home I think they can start bidding the dollar up again. Dollar/yen is still very, very bid," said Hans Bowman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank.
The dollar dipped under 1.83 marks before rebounding. But its more vigorous gains, versus the yen, came with with the help of a reinvigorated mark/yen.
At noon, the dollar was trading at 1.8320/30 marks, up from its 1.8315/25 open. Dollar/yen stood at 117.94/99, above 117.60/65 at the open, then jumped to 118.27.
The 118 level was considered a key bullish pivot level for dollar/yen, coinciding with the 200-day moving average.

Both the yen and sterling benefitted from the mark's ongoing correction from its recent broad-based plummet. Gains in dollar/yen as well as dollar/mark's early weakness were by amplified by mark/yen's advance to a session high of 64.44.
Sterling/mark continued its breathtaking pullback, hitting a low of 2.9745 in New York before bouncing a bit.

"Most of it is the D-mark on crosses," said Mike Malpede, a currency analyst at Refco Group Ltd. "There were a couple of comments made overseas from one of the German "wise men" that indicated that the Bundesbank may be considering intervention."
But few expect a lasting reprieve for the mark, with the U.S. economic backdrop -- steady growth, attractive yields and few signs of inflation -- seen fueling more gains for the greenback.
A modest rise in second-quarter U.S. labor costs reported on Tuesday, was good news but had little impact on the dollar.

The Labor Department said its Employment Cost Index rose 0.8 percent, as expected, last quarter, following a 0.6-percent first-quarter increase. The wage component grew at a slower rate, despite very tight U.S. labor markets.

"The U.S. economic fundamentals are better in the long term -- more stable than Germany's," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd. "In the coming years, people are still not sure how EMU will work out for the rest of Europe."
Dealers also said the budget pact struck between the White House and Capital Hill on Monday was underpinning the dollar.
In other trade, the dollar slipped to 1.5140/50 Swiss francs from 1.5155/60 at the open. It inched up to Canadian $1.3850/55 from C$1.3844/49.
